steps_summary: Step 1: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
Step 2: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
Step 3: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation

steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Colonic Polyps focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.dosing: Standard clinical care protocol under medical supervision.
drug_classes.pearls: Establish baseline clinical parameters and educate patient on trigger avoidance and early warning signs.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Dose optimization and complementary therapeutic escalation.
drug_classes.dosing: Titrate to target clinical biomarker thresholds under specialist guidance.
drug_classes.pearls: Evaluate patient compliance and consider secondary causes of treatment resistance.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Colonic Polyps require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Multidisciplinary tertiary intervention for refractory disease.
drug_classes.pearls: Consult subspecialty guidelines and consider therapeutic drug monitoring where applicable.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Colonic Polyps.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

special_populations.renal_impairment: Dose reduction or hydration protocols required for nephrotoxic antineoplastics (cisplatin, methotrexate).
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Monitor total bilirubin, transaminases, and alkaline phosphatase before each chemotherapy cycle.
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Chemotherapy contraindicated in first trimester; multidisciplinary tumor board consultation required.
special_populations.elderly: Comprehensive geriatric assessment to balance treatment efficacy against myelosuppression and cardiac toxicity.

style_3_monograph.summary: What are colonic polyps? Colonic polyps are growths on the inner lining of your colon or rectum. The rectum is the last part of your large intestine. Polyps are common in adults, especially as you get older. You can have one or more polyps. There are different types of polyps. Most are benign (noncancerous), but some are precancerous and may turn into cancer over time. Finding and removing polyps can help prevent colorectal cancer . During a procedure called a colonoscopy , your health care provider can examine your colon and remove any polyps. Who is more likely to develop colonic polyps? Anyone can get polyps, but they are more common in men and older adults. There are certain factors that may raise your risk of developing colonic polyps: Being age 45 or older Having had polyps before Having a family history of polyps or colorectal cancer Having inflammatory bowel disease, such as ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease Having obesity Smoking What causes colonic polyps? The cause of colonic polyps is unknown. It's believed that age, family history, and lifestyle may all play a role. What are the symptoms of colonic polyps? Most colonic polyps do not cause symptoms. If you do have symptoms, they may include: Bleeding from your rectum. You might see blood on your underwear or on toilet paper after a bowel movement (poop). Blood in your stool (poop). Blood may appear as red streaks or make stool look black. Fatigue . Bleeding from polyps can cause anemia , which means you don't have enough red blood cells. Anemia can make you feel tired. Changes in your bowel habits . This could include constipation or diarrhea that lasts more than a week. Many other health problems can also cause these symptoms. But if you notice bleeding from your rectum or blood in your stool, contact your provider right away. How are colonic polyps diagnosed? Providers use tests and procedures to find colonic polyps. Screening tests look for polyps or colorectal cancer in people who do not have any symptoms. These tests include: Colonoscopy , which uses a thin tube with a light and tiny camera to look inside your rectum and colon. Flexible sigmoidoscopy , which uses a thin tube with a light and tiny camera to check your rectum and the lower part of your colon (sigmoid colon). Virtual colonoscopy , which uses x-rays and a computer to create images of your colon. If the test finds a possible polyp, you will usually need a colonoscopy. Stool tests , which look for blood or other signs of colorectal cancer. An abnormal result may require you to have a follow-up colonoscopy. Most adults should start colorectal cancer screening at age 45. If you are more likely to get polyps or colorectal cancer, your provider may suggest starting sooner or testing more often. What are the treatments for colonic polyps? Most polyps can be removed during a colonoscopy or flexible sigmoidoscopy. The polyps are then tested for cancer. Rarely, you may need surgery to remove a large polyp or part of your colon if it can't be removed during one of these procedures. Can colonic polyps be prevented? There is no way to prevent colonic polyps, but healthy lifestyle habits may help lower your risk: Eating a healthy diet that includes fruits, vegetables, and other foods high in fiber Limiting highly processed and fried foods Getting regular exercise Maintaining a healthy weight Quitting smoking (or not starting) Getting screened is one of the best ways to find colonic polyps, so they can be removed before they become cancerous. NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
